title: The Price of a Cup of Buttermilk

full_text:
On a scorching summer afternoon, an elderly village woman named Gangamma walked three miles carrying a heavy earthen pot of fresh, cool buttermilk seasoned with curry leaves and ginger to the royal plaza. She sold cups of buttermilk for a single copper coin to parched porters and travelers.

An arrogant and haughty courtier named Somappa, dressed in lavish silk robes, strutted past. He demanded a large brass cup of cold buttermilk, drank it in one thirsty gulp, and tossed the cup back without paying.
When Gangamma asked for her copper coin, Somappa sneered:
'Old hag! Thou shouldst be honored that an imperial courtier drank from thy dirty earthen pot! Away from my path before I have my servants overturn thy stall!'

Gangamma began to weep. Tenali Raman, who was walking across the plaza, witnessed the injustice.
Tenali gently wiped the old woman's tears: 'Mother, sit in the shade. Somappa shall pay for thy buttermilk with interest.'

Tenali hurried to the palace and entered King Krishnadevaraya's audience hall, where Somappa was boasting of his lineage.
Tenali bowed:
'Maharaj, today I observed a miraculous demonstration of ancient culinary alchemy in the marketplace! Courtier Somappa has mastered the secret art of churning buttermilk so efficiently that a single cup can generate the strength of ten elephants!
He claims that churning butter is so effortless that he can churn an entire barrel of thick cream within two hours without breaking a sweat!'

The King, intrigued, looked at Somappa: 'Is this true, Somappa?'
Somappa, too proud to contradict Tenali in the presence of the Emperor, puffed out his chest: 'Of course, Your Majesty! For an aristocrat of my vigor, manual churning is child's play!'

Tenali smiled: 'Splendid! The palace kitchen has four barrels of thick buffalo curd waiting to be churned for tonight’s banquet. Let Somappa demonstrate his prowess before the court!'

A massive wooden churn and heavy rope were set up in the hot palace courtyard.
Somappa was forced to take off his fine silk coat and grip the rough hemp ropes.
For two grueling hours under the blazing afternoon sun, Somappa pulled and hauled, back and forth, back and forth!
His soft, unaccustomed hands blistered, his silk dhoti was splattered with sour cream, his breath came in ragged wheezes, and sweat poured like rain into his eyes!
Whenever he stopped, Tenali called out cheerfully:
'Keep pulling, noble courtier! The King is watching from the balcony!'

By the time the golden butter finally separated, Somappa collapsed onto the stone floor, completely exhausted, clutching his blistered palms.
Tenali handed him a cup of cold water and said softly:
'Now, Somappa, thou knowest what sweat, toil, and blistered hands go into making a single pot of buttermilk.
When poor old Gangamma walks three miles in the sun carrying her pot, a single copper coin is not just money; it is her very life and dignity.'

Somappa, humiliated and genuinely remorseful, reached into his purse and handed Gangamma ten gold coins for her cup of buttermilk.
The King praised Tenali’s lesson in the dignity of labor, decreeing that working artisans and vendors must be treated with unwavering courtesy throughout the empire.
moral: Arrogant nobility who despise the hard labor of working women are humbled when forced to sweat at the churn.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Price of Buttermilk"?
options: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
